When a lender takes back a home, the record can look like a sale

Foreclosure deeds can carry a lender’s bid or a cancelled debt, and most reach the city’s sales file as if they were prices. In the Bronx, counting them shifts the 2010 house-price index by about a tenth.

By Pablo Loschi1 October 2026Updated 15 November 20265 min readSources & methods

When a lender takes back a house at foreclosure, the deed often records the lender’s bid or the cancelled debt—sometimes right down to the cent. Much of the time, that figure passes straight into New York City's public sales file looking just like an ordinary home sale.

What this means when checking a price

Before relying on a distressed comparable price, open the deed and check who took title. A bank bid or discharged debt is a legal accounting figure, not necessarily a negotiated market price.

Across 1.47 million deed-family records in Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens (2003–2025), I flagged 16,655 lender-related deeds whose recorded amount can follow a statutory tax formula rather than a market bargain. Roughly 62% survive standard price and parcel filters, so I tested how a repeat-sales house index shifts when pairs touching them are excluded.

Citywide across the four boroughs, the raw and screened indices differ by up to 3.7 log points (roughly 4%) in the third quarter of 2010. Rather than claiming a single "true" price level, that gap shows how sensitive public indices are to leaving legal-rule amounts in.

Where foreclosures clustered, the shift is much sharper. In the Bronx—where 11% of repeat-sale pairs touch a flagged deed—keeping them lifts the 2010Q3 index by 10.9 log points (roughly 11%; 95% interval 6.6 to 14.7) compared with the screened path.

From a legal amount to a sales record

A foreclosure auction can hand a property to the lender that foreclosed. An owner can also sign a property over to a lender to avoid finishing the foreclosure. Neither is the kind of negotiated sale to a new household that a price index is meant to track.

New York's transfer-tax rules can set the recorded amount by what those instruments do legally. To find them, the study reads the type of instrument and who the parties are. A low amount or a bank-sounding name is not enough on its own.

The flagged deeds stand out in other ways too. About 70% of them record an amount with cents, against about 6% of ordinary deeds, and about 55% end up in repeat-sale pairs, against 27%. Neither pattern is enough to classify a deed by itself.

Of the flagged deeds from 2016 to 2025, about 94% to 95% show up in the city's public sales file at the same amount. The figure leaves the land registry and enters the data that researchers and websites use.

The timing changes more clearly than the crash depth

With the flagged transfers included, the index runs higher in parts of 2009 and 2010 and lower through 2011 and 2012. That moves the timing of the measured housing cycle.

The main 3.69-log-point gap has a 95% band of 1.59 to 5.78 that holds across the whole quarterly path. A narrower definition of flagged deeds still gives a maximum gap of about 2.6 log points (band 0.88 to 4.37), and counting only sales where both ends are houses gives 3.6.

The uncertainty chart above covers every quarter and six deed definitions at once on that stricter sample, guarding against cherry-picking a single peak quarter (conditional on the classification and matching rules). Dropping matched sets of ordinary sales moves the path too, though the gap changes with how those comparisons are constructed.

The overall depth of the crash barely moves: the peak-to-trough difference is under one log point (under 1%), and its interval includes zero. What the flagged deeds change is when the crash shows up.

A model that uses property details shows it too

The paper also tests a hedonic index built from sale amounts and property features. On the shared sample, screening changes its third-quarter 2010 value by 2.07 log points under the main definition and 1.55 under the narrow one, with both bands above zero there. Later in the decade it diverges from the repeat-sales path, consistent with sale pairing driving part of the later shortfall.

Reading the field before using the number

The 40 human deed readings leave real classification uncertainty—folding label error into the model moves the 2010 gap to 2.25 log points (95% range −0.21 to +4.53), and alternative date or pairing choices can attenuate or reverse it. Public screening helps diagnose index noise rather than producing a gold-standard market price series.

Even so, opening the underlying deed before citing a distressed price as a market comparable keeps a legal debt calculation from masquerading as an arm’s-length sale. All classifier rules and replication scripts are public in the paper’s dataset and archive.

Sources and methods

This article explains Pablo Loschi's own research in When a Deed Is Not a Market Sale, full paper (PDF) (v1.0.17, 10.5281/zenodo.24273577). The fixed-label chart series were first released in version 1.0.6, and the Bronx figure in version 1.0.9; all remain unchanged in v1.0.15 and are archived under v1.0.17 alongside the 14-page Measurement Note. Note that the 40 human document readings in the paper do not validate the 316 earlier AI classifications, and the chart bands condition on fixed labels without classification-rate uncertainty.
